I believe that forcing people to vote could lead to a lot of uninformed or unenthusiastic votes, which wouldn't really add any value to the democratic process. Plus, what about people who genuinely don't feel represented by any of the options, or who are disillusioned with politics altogether? Shouldn't they have the right to abstain if that's how they feel? I think we should focus on encouraging people to engage with politics and making voting more accessible, rather than making it compulsory. That way, people can make their own informed decisions about whether or not to participate.

I think we should definitely strive to create safer, more supportive environments, but to say we can completely eliminate bullying feels like a pipe dream to me.

I've seen it time and time again, where a free press has exposed injustices and sparked real change. Without it, I think we'd be lost, with no way to hold our leaders accountable for their actions. It's not always comfortable, and sometimes the press gets it wrong, but the alternative - a press that's muzzled or controlled - is just too scary to contemplate.

For me, it's about making sure people have a bit more life experience and emotional maturity before they're making decisions that affect the whole country. I mean, I look back at my own teenage years and I was still figuring out who I was and what I believed in - I don't think I would have been ready to vote in a way that truly represented my values. By 18, you've had a bit more time to develop your own thoughts and opinions, and you're more likely to be independent and making your own decisions. It just feels like a more responsible age to be given the power to shape our collective future.

I think we should focus on finding a balance between providing kids with access to technology and teaching them how to use it responsibly, rather than just handing each one their own computer.

situation: Austerity is the best policy in an economic downturn.
text: Honestly, as a woman, I just can't get on board with the idea that austerity is the best policy in an economic downturn. To me, it feels like we're essentially asking the people who are already struggling the most to tighten their belts even further, while those who have more wealth and resources are barely affected. It doesn't seem fair or sustainable. I think about my own family and friends who have been hit hard by economic downturns in the past - the ones who lost their jobs, had to choose between paying rent or buying groceries, and had to put their dreams on hold. Austerity policies would have only made things worse for them. Instead, I think we should be investing in programs that support the most vulnerable members of our society, stimulating growth, and creating jobs. That's how we can really get out of an economic downturn, not by cutting back on the things that matter most.

I'm not trying to be insensitive, but I just don't think the legal system should be involved in something like this.

It's an investment in our community, and I truly believe it would make a huge difference in people's lives, including mine.

situation: It would be better to have a President rather than a Prime Minister.
text: Honestly, as a woman, I've always thought that having a President would be a more effective system than a Prime Minister. To me, it seems like a President has a clearer mandate from the people, you know? They're directly elected by the population, so there's no question about who they're accountable to. With a Prime Minister, it's often more about party politics and who can command the most support in the legislature. I think that can lead to a lot of behind-the-scenes deals and compromises that might not be in the best interest of the country as a whole. A President, on the other hand, has to be more of a unifying figure, and I think that could really help to bring people together and give them a sense of stability and direction. Plus, it just feels more straightforward and transparent to me - one person, directly elected, making the big decisions. It's easier to know who to hold accountable, you know?

text: Honestly, as a woman, I just don't think having a President is inherently better than having a Prime Minister. To me, it seems like the effectiveness of a leader isn't determined by their title, but by the system they're working within and their own abilities. I've seen countries with Prime Ministers that are incredibly stable and successful, and others with Presidents that are struggling. It feels like we're focusing on the wrong thing if we're debating titles rather than the actual policies and values that a leader represents. Plus, I think the idea of a President often comes with a lot of extra powers and expectations that can be really problematic - it can create a sense of authoritarianism and make it harder for other branches of government to hold them accountable. Give me a fair, competent, and compassionate Prime Minister any day over a President with too much power and not enough checks and balances.

I mean, we all need healthcare, but we all eat food too - and let's be real, some of the foods that are worst for us are also the cheapest and most readily available. If we could use that to our advantage and generate revenue for the NHS, I think it could be a really clever move. Plus, it might even encourage people to make healthier choices, which would be a win-win. I know it's not a simple solution, but I think it's worth exploring - anything that could take some of the pressure off our amazing NHS staff and ensure everyone gets the care they need has got to be worth considering.

situation: It should be easier to get divorce in the UK.
text: Honestly, as a woman, I think it's about time we made divorce easier to get in the UK. I've seen friends go through absolutely miserable marriages, staying together just because the process of splitting up is so daunting and expensive. It's not just the financial burden, it's the emotional toll of having to prove that your marriage has 'irreconcilable differences' or whatever the legal jargon is. I think if people want to end their marriage, they should be able to do so without having to jump through hoops or feel guilty about it. It's their life, after all. Making divorce easier wouldn't be about encouraging people to give up on their relationships, but about acknowledging that sometimes things just don't work out, and that's okay.

And then to be given a temporary reprieve, but still live with the uncertainty of not knowing if you'll be allowed to stay long-term... it's just so unfair. It's the right thing to do, morally and ethically. We should be welcoming and compassionate, not punitive and restrictive.

situation: The minimum age for driving should be increased from 17 to 18.
text: Honestly, as a woman, I think increasing the minimum driving age to 18 makes a lot of sense to me. When I look back, I was nowhere near ready to drive at 17 - I was still figuring out how to navigate school and social stuff, and adding driving to the mix just seemed like too much. I've seen friends get into accidents or lose their licenses because they just weren't mature enough to handle the responsibility. By 18, you've usually had a bit more time to develop some independence and learn how to prioritize, which I think is crucial for safe driving. Plus, it would give new drivers an extra year to observe and learn from others, which can only be a good thing. For me, it's just common sense - if we can wait a year for someone to be considered an adult in so many other areas of life, why not driving too?

It just seems like we should be focusing on making a difference where we can have more control and see tangible results.

I think we should be focusing on creating jobs, improving education, and supporting small businesses instead of just handing out a monthly check. It's not that I don't want to help people who are struggling, it's just that I think there are better, more effective ways to do it.

situation: Young people should be allowed to vote in elections.
text: Honestly, as a woman, I'm not sure I agree with letting young people vote in elections. To me, voting is a huge responsibility that requires a certain level of life experience and understanding of the world. I think a lot of young people, especially those under 18, are still figuring out their own beliefs and values, and may not have the emotional maturity to make informed decisions that affect the entire country. I'm not saying they're not capable or intelligent, but I think it's a big ask to expect them to have the same level of perspective and wisdom as someone who's been around for a few more years. Plus, at that age, you're still being influenced by your parents, teachers, and peers, and I worry that their votes might not be entirely their own. I just think it's better to wait until they've had a chance to develop a bit more independence and worldly experience before giving them the right to vote.

Plus, it's just a matter of respect for others - if I'm trying to escape into a book or work on a project, I don't want to be interrupted by someone's loud conversation. I think signs would be a gentle reminder for people to be considerate of those around them, and it would make the library a much more enjoyable and productive space for everyone.

text: Honestly, as a woman, I think most school exams are too easy. I've taken my fair share of tests and exams, and often I've felt like I'm just regurgitating information I memorized the night before, rather than actually applying what I've learned. It's like, what's the point of education if we're not being challenged to think critically and solve problems? I've had friends who have barely studied and still managed to pass with flying colors, which makes me wonder if the exams are really doing their job. I think if exams were more rigorous, it would push us to work harder and actually understand the material, rather than just skimming the surface.

I'm not saying technology doesn't have its benefits, but I do think we need to find a healthier balance and make a conscious effort to disconnect from it all sometimes.

situation: We should outlaw or severely restrict facial recognition software.
text: Honestly, as a woman, I'm really in favour of outlawing or severely restricting facial recognition software. For me, it's a huge invasion of privacy - I mean, think about it, our faces are literally the most identifying feature we have, and the idea that they can be tracked and monitored without our consent is just creepy. I've heard stories about people being wrongly identified and detained because of faulty facial recognition, and that's just terrifying. Plus, it feels like it's always the most vulnerable people who are affected by this kind of technology - minorities, protesters, people who are already marginalized. I just don't think the benefits of facial recognition outweigh the risks, and I think we need to prioritize our right to privacy and anonymity in public spaces.

It's not about pushing any particular agenda, it's just about giving kids the language and the space to be who they are, without fear of judgment or rejection.
